rv.q: At 88, Churchill remains sharp as ever.
To express this, as she does, in works that get briefer and more concentrated with each year makes her the most pungent theatrical prophet alive today.
It's more of a politicised sketch than a play, but it's hugely welcome that at 88, Churchill's urge to question the world theatrically remains undimmed.
Within the limited arc of her character, O’Flynn is excellent, her bright-eyed zeal swiftly hollowed out.
As a satire on Donald Trump’s presidency, it’s of passing interest.
Caryl Churchill’s new play, Triumph, is a gem.
And there's a week to go still for Sam Yates's knockout revival of Clifford Odets' boxing drama Golden Boy, which will live on in cinemas following the run via NT Live starting Nov. 5.
Even for 15 minutes, her voice needs to be heard.
A superb, substantial sliver from a master who can still cut it, gleaming and toothed and entire unto itself.
Proof that even at 88, one of the finest playwrights of the last few decades still has plenty to say.
Triumph is incredibly thought-provoking and impactful for those reasons.

The conceit of quoting Suetonius is inspired, allowing Churchill to make brutal connections between the lies, cruelty, and decadence of the last days of Ancient Rome and the horror show we find ourselves in under the megalomaniac rule of a very current leader.
This short play packs a punch and Churchill once again proves why she is one of the most celebrated playwrights of political drama and the British theatre industry.
We get Churchill’s allegory and the abuse of power and the dangers of populism, and while there is that flash of the human impact on O’Flynn, maybe it’s a little too focused on the big picture.
There’s nothing enlightening about being reminded of the past actions of the Trump administration through these parallels, even if the act of recollection is entertaining in and of itself.
It is a clever and amusing device, but the play amounts to little more than a short skit of the kind more commonly associated with the Fringe.
Instead, Churchill chooses cliché over controversy and ultimately offers precious little.

cn.t: Churchill's 20-minute satire draws sharp parallels between Roman emperors and Trump's White House to mostly positive reviews, though some critics find the concept too brief or unoriginal to fully triumph.
